title: Bayesian Inference: Practice Exercises
content:
# Bayesian Inference: Updating Beliefs with Bayes' Rule

**Core idea.** Bayesian inference combines a *prior* belief about a hypothesis with a *likelihood* of the observed data to produce a *posterior*:

P(h | d) = P(d | h) · P(h) / P(d)

where P(d) is the total probability of the data, found by summing P(d | h)·P(h) over all hypotheses.

**Worked reference (umbrella example).** Prior: P(rainy) = 0.15, P(dry) = 0.85. Likelihoods: P(umbrella | rainy) = 0.30, P(umbrella | dry) = 0.05. Joint probabilities: rainy & umbrella = 0.045, dry & umbrella = 0.0425, so P(umbrella) = 0.0875. Posterior: P(rainy | umbrella) = 0.045 / 0.0875 ≈ 0.514 — the observation of the umbrella roughly triples the probability of rain from 15% to about 51%.

---

## Exercise 1 — The umbrella problem, continued

Using the same setup as above (P(rainy) = 0.15, P(umbrella | rainy) = 0.30, P(umbrella | dry) = 0.05), suppose instead you observe that Danielle is **not** carrying an umbrella.

1. Build the full joint probability table for the four possibilities (rainy/dry × umbrella/no-umbrella) and verify the row and column totals sum to 1.
2. Compute P(no-umbrella).
3. Use Bayes' rule to find the posterior P(rainy | no-umbrella). Does the observation lower or raise your belief that it is raining, compared with the prior of 0.15?

**Solution sketch.** Joint table: rainy & umbrella = 0.045, rainy & no-umbrella = 0.105, dry & umbrella = 0.0425, dry & no-umbrella = 0.8075. P(no-umbrella) = 0.105 + 0.8075 = 0.9125. Posterior: P(rainy | no-umbrella) = 0.105 / 0.9125 ≈ 0.115 — the observation lowers the probability of rain below the prior.

## Exercise 2 — Medical test (base-rate reasoning)

A test correctly identifies a disease in 95% of people who have it, and correctly identifies no disease in 94% of people who do not have it. In the population, 3% of people have the disease. What is the probability that you have the disease if you test positive?

**Solution sketch.** Let D = has disease, + = positive test. Prior P(D) = 0.03; likelihoods P(+ | D) = 0.95, P(+ | no D) = 0.06. Then P(+) = 0.95 × 0.03 + 0.06 × 0.97 = 0.0285 + 0.0582 = 0.0867, so P(D | +) = 0.0285 / 0.0867 ≈ 0.329. Despite the accurate test, only about a third of positive results are true positives — a classic demonstration of why the prior (base rate) matters in Bayesian inference.

---

**Takeaway.** In both exercises the pattern is identical: multiply each prior by its likelihood, normalize by the total probability of the data, and read off the posterior. Surprising data (an umbrella on a dry day, a positive test for a rare disease) can still leave the posterior far from certain.
